> **What this case shows** — from resting ECG alone, the ecosystem recovers the
> textbook signature of cardiovascular **aging**: overall heart-rate variability
> is much lower in the elderly than in the young (median total power **1021 vs
> 3596 ms²**, Wilcoxon *p* = **0.0004**), and the high-frequency **vagal** power
> is lower too (*p* = **0.004**). **What reproduces, and what doesn't** — the
> **magnitude** of HRV separates the age groups; the **balance ratios**
> (LF/HF, HFnu) and the **resting heart rate** do **not** (*p* = 0.66 / 0.34) —
> aging shows up as *less variability*, not a shifted ratio or a faster pulse.
> One elderly record was set aside because the pipeline flagged frequent ectopy
> (frequency-domain HRV is undefined there). **How to read it** — left, total HRV
> power per subject by age group (log scale); right, the normalised vagal ratio,
> which overlaps.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — answer *"how does autonomic control differ between groups?"* in
four moves: **load** each ECG → **detect** the beats → **form** the RR-interval
series → **spectrally summarise** it into LF / HF / total power, then compare
groups.
**Way of thinking** — frequency-domain HRV needs a *stationary* segment, so fix
one analysis window for everyone; separate HRV **magnitude** from **balance**
(they can behave differently); use a rank test for the wide, skewed spread of HRV
across people; and let the rhythm check refuse records where the metric is
undefined rather than reporting a number anyway.
**Ecosystem usage** — chain one function per role, I/O → analysis
(`readWFDB` → `ecgDetectRpeaks` → `ecgRRintervals` → `ecgHRVfreq`). The final
section turns this into a step-by-step you can adapt to your own ECG.
:::

## Proposition

On real resting ECG, frequency-domain HRV separates young from elderly by
**magnitude**: median total power **3596 ms² (young)** vs **1021 ms² (elderly)**
(*p* = 0.0004) and lower HF vagal power in the elderly (*p* = 0.004) — while the
normalised balance (LF/HF, HFnu) and the resting mean heart rate do **not**
differ between the groups.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from the dataset's own design.** Fantasia was assembled to
study **how autonomic control of the heart changes with age**: 20 rigorously
screened healthy subjects — **10 young** (21–34 y) and **10 elderly** (68–81 y) —
each recorded at rest for two hours, hand-checked for clean sinus rhythm (Iyengar
et al., 1996). The expected physiology is well established: with age the heart
loses **variability**, especially in the **high-frequency** band that reflects
**parasympathetic (vagal)** control (Task Force, 1996). So we ask the dataset's
own question: does frequency-domain HRV, computed by the ecosystem, recover the
young-vs-elderly difference — and where exactly does the difference live?

## Challenge & approach

Frequency-domain HRV is only meaningful on a **stationary** segment, and it is
easily corrupted by missed or extra beats. So we fix one analysis window for
every subject — a **10-minute** resting segment (t = 300–900 s, skipping the
recording onset) — detect the beats, form the RR series, and take its power
spectrum:

```
readWFDB → [ECG channel, 10-min window] → ecgDetectRpeaks(pan_tompkins) → ecgRRintervals → ecgHRVfreq(welch)
```

`ecgHRVfreq()` splits the RR spectrum into VLF / LF / **HF** bands and reports
**total power**, the **LF/HF** ratio, and normalised units. We compare the two
age groups with a **Wilcoxon rank-sum** test — robust to the wide, skewed spread
of HRV across people. Its built-in **rhythm check** refuses records with frequent
ectopy (where the metric is undefined) rather than returning a misleading number.

## Data

**Fantasia Database** (PhysioNet) — public
(<https://physionet.org/content/fantasia/1.0.0/>), ODbL. Records **f1y01–f1y10**
(young) and **f1o01–f1o10** (elderly), resting ECG at 250 Hz. The exact records
(with checksums and ages) are in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json). *Iyengar N, et al.
Am J Physiol. 1996;271(4):R1078–84; Goldberger AL, et al. Circulation.
2000;101(23):e215–20.*

## Results

![Left: total HRV power per subject by age group (log scale) — the young cohort sits far above the elderly (Wilcoxon p = 0.0004). Right: the normalised HF power (HFnu, the vagal balance index) overlaps between groups (p = 0.66). Aging lowers the amount of variability, not the balance ratio.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* each point is one subject; the box spans the interquartile
range. On the left the two groups barely overlap (a real age effect); on the
right they sit on top of each other (no effect).

**Group comparison**
([`artifacts/hrv_group_summary.csv`](artifacts/hrv_group_summary.csv)):

| HRV metric | Young median | Elderly median | Wilcoxon *p* | Separates? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Total power** (ms²) | **3596** | **1021** | **0.0004** | **yes** |
| **HF (vagal) power** (ms²) | 802 | 233 | **0.004** | **yes** |
| LF/HF ratio | 1.92 | 1.67 | 0.66 | no |
| HFnu (normalised HF) | 34.2 | 37.5 | 0.66 | no |
| Resting mean HR (bpm) | 62.0 | 59.5 | 0.34 | no |

The **magnitude** of HRV — total power and HF vagal power — is markedly lower in
the elderly; the **balance ratios** and the **resting heart rate** do not
distinguish the groups. One elderly record (**f1o09**) was flagged for frequent
ectopy by the rhythm check and excluded from the frequency metrics, leaving
**10 young vs 9 elderly** for those rows
([`artifacts/hrv_per_subject.csv`](artifacts/hrv_per_subject.csv)).

## Conclusion

On public resting ECG the ecosystem recovers the classic autonomic-aging finding
— less heart-rate variability, and specifically less high-frequency vagal power,
in the elderly — while honestly showing where the effect is **not**: the
normalised balance ratios and the mean heart rate. The transferable lesson is to
separate HRV **magnitude** from **balance**, fix a stationary window, use a rank
test for skewed physiological spread, and trust a pipeline that refuses to score
a record it cannot score correctly.

## Open questions

The normalised sympathovagal indices (LF/HF, HFnu) do not distinguish the age
groups here even though absolute power does — consistent with normalisation
removing the very magnitude collapse that carries the aging signal. Whether a
longer or multi-window analysis would reveal a balance shift is a genuine
question; the magnitude result is the robust one and is what we claim.
Documented, not escalated.

## Using this in your own analysis

This case is a worked example of a **frequency-domain HRV group comparison** —
the pattern for any "does autonomic control differ between these conditions or
groups?" question.

**The general recipe** (four steps):

1. **Load** each ECG record and pick the ECG channel.
2. **Detect** the R-peaks and **form** the RR-interval series on a *fixed,
   stationary* window (same for every record).
3. **Spectrally summarise** the RR series into LF / HF / total power with
   `ecgHRVfreq()`.
4. **Compare** groups with a rank-based test, and split *magnitude* from
   *balance* — they can move independently.

**Which functions, and how they compose.** Each step is one ecosystem function,
picked by *role* — I/O → analysis:

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| load a WFDB ECG record | `readWFDB()` | PhysioIO |
| detect the R-peaks | `ecgDetectRpeaks()` | PhysioECG |
| beat-to-beat RR-interval series | `ecgRRintervals()` | PhysioECG |
| frequency-domain HRV (LF/HF/total) | `ecgHRVfreq()` | PhysioECG |

They chain because each consumes what the previous returns — the shared
`PhysioExperiment` and the RR data frame carry the signal from I/O to the HRV
spectrum, so you compose by naming the steps.

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **Analysis window** — frequency-domain HRV assumes stationarity; use a fixed
  short-term window (≥ 5 min; here 10 min) rather than a whole ambulatory record,
  and the *same* window for every subject.
- **Detector (`method`)** — `pan_tompkins` is a robust default for clean ECG;
  match the detector to lead quality.
- **`method = "welch"`** in `ecgHRVfreq()` — a stable periodogram estimate of the
  RR spectrum; `"lomb"` handles unevenly sampled RR without interpolation.
- **`rhythm_check = TRUE`** — leave it on: it returns `NA` on records with
  frequent ectopy, where frequency-domain HRV is undefined, instead of a
  misleading number.

**Applying it to your own hypothesis.** Swap in your own two groups or conditions
(rest vs stress, patients vs controls, pre vs post), keep the detect → RR →
`ecgHRVfreq` recipe on a fixed window, and compare **total power / HF** for the
magnitude question separately from **LF/HF** for the balance question. The same
detect-and-summarise-the-heartbeat pipeline underlies the resting heart-rate and
time-domain HRV cases on MIT-BIH
([`ecg-hr-spectrum-mitbih`](../ecg-hr-spectrum-mitbih/),
[`ecg-hrv-mitbih`](../ecg-hrv-mitbih/)).

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioIO); library(PhysioECG)

hrv_window <- function(rec, t0 = 300, dur = 600) {
  pe  <- readWFDB(rec)                                       # Fantasia: RESP + ECG @ 250 Hz
  sr  <- samplingRate(pe)
  ecg <- pe[, which(toupper(SummarizedExperiment::colData(pe)$label) == "ECG")]
  seg <- ecg[(t0 * sr + 1):((t0 + dur) * sr), ]             # fixed 10-min window
  pk  <- ecgDetectRpeaks(seg, method = "pan_tompkins")      # R-peaks
  rr  <- ecgRRintervals(seg, pk)                            # RR series
  ecgHRVfreq(rr, method = "welch")                          # LF / HF / total power
}

young   <- hrv_window("f1y01")$total_power                 # high
elderly <- hrv_window("f1o01")$total_power                 # low
```

**Auditing the numbers.** For readers who want to verify rather than trust: every
subject's HRV metrics and the group medians and *p*-values live in
[`artifacts/`](artifacts/), and `audit.py` re-derives the medians from the
per-subject table and re-checks each *p*-value and the young > elderly direction.
